meta.name: 121 - Mixed Overdose with Partial Naloxone Response

history.hpi: Roommate returned home and found the patient unresponsive on the bathroom floor, next to a spoon and a syringe. Roommate estimates he was last seen normal about an hour ago. Patient is unresponsive to voice, breathing is slow and shallow with occasional snoring respirations.
pastMedical: Prior opioid use disorder, one prior overdose two years ago
history.lastOralIntake: Unknown, roommate reports patient ate dinner about 3 hours ago
history.events: Roommate found patient unresponsive on the bathroom floor with drug paraphernalia nearby and called 911 immediately

scene.location: Second-floor apartment bathroom, patient supine on the floor between the toilet and tub
scene.safety: Uncapped syringe visible on the floor near the patient; roommate cooperative and away from immediate area
scene.bystanders: Roommate present, found the patient and called 911, provides history of prior opioid use
visualCues: Uncapped syringe and spoon with residue on the bathroom floor
Empty pill bottle (unlabeled) also visible near the sink

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a 32-year-old male unresponsive on the bathroom floor with slow, shallow, snoring respirations, cyanotic lips, and pinpoint pupils. Drug paraphernalia and an unlabeled pill bottle are visible, raising concern for a mixed ingestion rather than opioids alone.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Partially obstructed, snoring respirations from tongue occlusion
otherFindings: Track marks on both antecubital areas
Uncapped syringe and unlabeled pill bottle nearby

expectedActions.shortAction: Open airway (jaw thrust/NPA) and begin two-person BVM with PEEP before giving naloxone
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Therapeutic interventions to support the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation should be initiated prior to the administration of naloxone
expectedActions.rationale: Airway and ventilation support must not be delayed waiting for naloxone to take effect.

expectedActions.shortAction: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV, titrate incrementally to effect (not weight-based; fixed adult range)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The typical initial adult dose ranges between Naloxone 0.4–2 mg IV, IM, up to a dose of 4 mg IN or 5 mg ETT. The administration of the initial dose or subsequent doses can be incrementally titrated until respiratory depression is reversed
expectedActions.rationale: Titrating in small increments reverses respiratory depression while minimizing the risk of precipitated withdrawal.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose and screen for other causes of AMS (hypoxia, hypotension, head trauma)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess the patient for other etiologies of altered mental status including hypoxia (pulse oximetry less than 94%), hypoglycemia, hypotension, and traumatic head injury
expectedActions.rationale: A mixed ingestion or coexisting cause may explain incomplete response to naloxone alone.

transitions.condition: Crew opens and supports the airway with BVM ventilation and PEEP before administering naloxone, then titrates naloxone incrementally IV while checking BGL and screening for other causes of altered mental status.
Crew administers a full rapid dose of naloxone immediately without first opening the airway or supporting ventilation with BVM.

phases.name: BVM started, naloxone titrated
phases.description: Crew opens the airway with a jaw thrust, inserts an NPA, and begins two-person BVM ventilation with PEEP prior to giving naloxone. Naloxone is then titrated in small incremental doses IV while the crew checks blood glucose and screens for other causes of altered mental status.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing airway obstruction and severe hypoventilation, the crew supports oxygenation and ventilation first, then titrates naloxone in small increments rather than pushing a large reversal dose.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent with NPA and jaw thrust, BVM-assisted
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Assisted via BVM with PEEP, spontaneous effort improving, less cyanotic
otherFindings: BGL 95 mg/dL, ruling out hypoglycemia as a contributing cause
No signs of head trauma on exam
Naloxone 0.4 mg IV given, repeated once for total 0.8 mg with gradual improvement in respiratory effort

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue BVM support rather than escalating to RSI, since ventilation remains effective
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Regardless of the doses of naloxone administered, airway management with provision of adequate oxygenation and ventilation is the primary goal in patients with confirmed or suspected opioid overdose
expectedActions.rationale: BVM is meeting oxygenation/ventilation goals, so advanced airway placement is not indicated at this time.

expectedActions.shortAction: Monitor closely for recurrent respiratory depression; naloxone effect is shorter than the opioid's duration
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The clinical opioid reversal effect of naloxone is limited and may end within an hour whereas opioids often have a duration of 4 hours or longer. Monitor the patient for recurrent respiratory depression and decreased mental status
expectedActions.rationale: Renarcotization can occur en route once the naloxone dose wears off before the opioid does.

transitions.condition: Respiratory effort improves but remains inadequate to protect the airway independently, consistent with a mixed ingestion; crew continues ventilatory support rather than repeatedly escalating naloxone.

phases.name: Partial response, BVM continued
phases.description: Respiratory drive improves partially but the patient still cannot protect his own airway reliably. The crew continues bag-valve-mask support with supplemental naloxone titration as needed, avoiding advanced airway placement since BVM remains effective, and transports with continuous reassessment for recurrent respiratory depression.
phases.triggerCondition: Naloxone and ventilatory support produce partial reversal, but incomplete response suggests a co-ingestant (e.g., benzodiazepine); the crew continues BVM support rather than pursuing RSI, since ventilation remains effective.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, maintaining with positioning and intermittent BVM support
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Spontaneous but shallow, 8/min, effectively assisted with BVM
otherFindings: Responds weakly to loud voice, does not yet follow commands
No recurrence of cyanosis with continued BVM support
Prepared for transport with ongoing reassessment for renarcotization

phases.name: Naloxone given before airway supported
phases.description: The crew pushes a full rapid dose of naloxone immediately, without first opening the airway or providing BVM support. The patient remains hypoxic during the delay, and as the naloxone takes effect he becomes acutely agitated from precipitated withdrawal while still poorly oxygenated.
phases.triggerCondition: Naloxone is given as a rapid, undiluted dose before the airway and breathing are supported; the patient remains hypoxic through the delay and then becomes combative from precipitated opioid withdrawal.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Thrashing, biting at airway adjuncts, difficult to manage
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Erratic, gasping, poorly coordinated with attempted BVM
otherFindings: Abrupt agitation and combativeness after rapid naloxone dose
SpO2 remains low due to delayed ventilatory support
Airway management now more difficult due to patient combativeness

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize precipitated withdrawal from rapid naloxone; resume BVM support and allow agitation to settle
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients with altered mental status secondary to an opioid overdose may become agitated or violent following naloxone administration due to opioid withdrawal therefore the goal is to use the lowest dose as possible to avoid precipitating withdrawal
expectedActions.rationale: Rapid, large-dose naloxone without prior ventilatory support risks both ongoing hypoxia and a combative, harder-to-manage patient.
